title: Application-Level Replication by Writing to Every Replica
pattern: Application code replicates data itself by issuing the same write to several nodes of one logical store (primary and read replica, master and DR clone, active/active cache or grid peers) instead of writing to the single owner and letting the store's replication propagate it.
why_bad: The store already replicates, so application writes collide with the replication stream: duplicate-key errors, broken sequences, or updates applied twice. Where the store does not replicate, the application has become the replication protocol without sequence numbers, catch-up or conflict resolution. A crash or partition between the writes leaves replicas silently missing data, and concurrent writers can apply updates to peers in opposite orders so the nodes diverge.
detection: Two or more handles to nodes of the same logical database, cache or grid (`primary`/`replica`, `master`/`clone`, `node_a`/`node_b`) and the same insert/update/put issued to each for the same record, outside the store's own replication or consensus client.
counterexample: Writes routed only to the primary or partition owner with reads served from replicas; client libraries that implement the store's own quorum protocol (e.g. Cassandra/Dynamo-style coordinators); deliberate fan-out to independent stores, which is the general dual-write problem rather than replication.
source: Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications* (2017), Ch. 5, pp. 152–156; Vaughn Vernon, *Implementing Domain-Driven Design* (2013), App. A, Fig. A.7, p. 641; Mark Richards & Neal Ford, *Fundamentals of Software Architecture* (2020), Ch. 15, pp. 216–217.
